meta.source: Hot Water Math editorial assumptions (documented on /methodology)
meta.notes: No government agency publishes a repair-or-replace rule for water heaters. These thresholds are our own, chosen to be conservative and stated openly so you can judge them: a leaking tank is always a replacement; otherwise replace when a repair costs more than half of a new unit, or when the unit has used three quarters of its typical life and the repair costs more than a quarter of a new unit.

repairOrReplace.note: Since audit fix F-08 (2026-11-14): a unit at or past the high end of its life range (data/lifespans.json) is "replace soon" whatever the repair costs; rusty hot water (always) or rumbling once the unit is old (ageShare of its typical life) moves the verdict one step toward replace, because Rheem lists both among the signs a heater should be replaced. The "old" share of typical life is data/lifespans.json statusBands.oldFrom, shared with the age calculator (audit F-09, 2026-11-14).

meta.source: Rheem, Water Heater Lifespan: When to Repair vs. Replace (March 25, 2026) and A. O. Smith Residential Electronic Thermostat Electric Water Heater Use and Care Guide (2021)
meta.note: Which symptoms point to a replacement and which to a part. Only a leak from the tank itself forces a replacement in the tool; the others are shown as guidance.

items.label: Water leaking from the tank itself
items.note: A leak from the tank body cannot be fixed; the heater has to be replaced. Check first that the water is not coming from a pipe, valve or fitting above it, because leaks are often in the plumbing, not the heater.
items.source: Rheem: "If the leak is from the tank itself, replacement is usually required." A. O. Smith: "Leaks are frequently in the plumbing system itself and not the water heater."

items.label: Drip at a valve, pipe or fitting
items.note: Small valve or fitting leaks are often repairable.
items.source: Rheem: "Small valve or fitting leaks may be repairable."

items.label: Rusty or discolored hot water
items.note: Rheem lists rusty or discolored hot water as a sign the heater should be replaced. Rusty water can also come from old pipes, so check whether the cold water is clear.
items.source: Rheem: "rusty or discolored hot water" is listed among the clear signs a water heater should be replaced.

items.label: Rumbling or popping noise
items.note: Persistent rumbling or popping comes from hardened sediment on the tank floor; Rheem counts it among the signs of replacement.
items.source: Rheem: "persistent rumbling or popping sounds caused by hardened sediment on the tank floor."

items.label: No hot water, or not enough
items.note: Often a heating element, thermostat or (on gas units) the ignition parts. Heating elements, thermostats and anode rods are designed to be replaced.
items.source: Rheem: "Heating elements, thermostats, and anode rods are all designed to be swapped out."

items.label: Relief valve dripping or discharging
items.note: The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve is a safety device. Never cap or plug it or its discharge pipe; have the cause checked.
items.source: A. O. Smith Use and Care Guide: "An explosion could occur if the T&P Relief Valve or discharge pipe is blocked. Do not cap or plug the T&P Relief Valve or discharge pipe."

items.label: Heater was in a flood
items.note: If the heater was flooded or its controls were under water, the manufacturer says the whole unit must be replaced.
items.source: A. O. Smith Use and Care Guide: "If the water heater is subjected to flood conditions or the thermostat(s) have been submerged in water, the entire water heater must be replaced."
